## [19] What Role for the Spatial Organisation of Human Societies to Modulate their Pressures on Biodiversity?
<hr />

{{< fa calendar-days >}}&nbsp; October 2026
<br/>{{< fa user >}}&nbsp; **Isabelle Boulangeat** (INRAE, France) 
<br/>{{< fa user >}}&nbsp; **Mohamed Hilal** (INRAE, France)
<br/>{{< fa user >}}&nbsp; **Cathleen Petit-Cailleux** (Kyoto University, France)
<br/>{{< fa globe >}}&nbsp; [SPATMAN](https://www.fondationbiodiversite.fr/en/the-frb-in-action/programs-and-projects/le-cesab/spatman/) project

<br/>

**Abstract**

Human pressures on biodiversity are influenced not just by the intensity of human 
activities, but also by their spatial organization. This is the main focus of 
the FRB-CESAB [SPATMAN](https://www.fondationbiodiversite.fr/en/the-frb-in-action/programs-and-projects/le-cesab/spatman/) project, which unites conservation ecologists, spatial 
ecologists, geographers, and economists to investigate how human pressures impact 
biodiversity by examining the characteristics of the human activities involved.

This webinar presents two subprojects. The first links the presence of sensitive 
species (birds, mammals, amphibians) to two dimensions of human pressures: 
(1) how humans have structured the landscape and (2) where people are or move 
(resident population, work mobility, tourism). This research is carried out on 
a 10×10 km grid, using machine learning in addition to linear models. Results 
emphasize a significant role for human mobility.

The second subproject maps, on a global scale, the scientific evidence regarding
direct human pressures on terrestrial biodiversity. It assesses among other 
criteria the frequency of different ecological scales in the studies and the 
types of human pressures or activities investigated. Using a corpus of nearly 
200,000 references, natural language processing tools identify thematic trends 
and knowledge gaps.

Together, these two approaches demonstrate how SPATMAN offers a new perspective 
on human pressures and their impacts on biodiversity.
